book.title: Biceps-related Shoulder Pain and Biceps Tendon Rupture

blocks.text: The **biceps brachii** has two heads. The **long head** passes through the bicipital groove at the front of the shoulder and attaches inside the joint to the top of the socket (the labrum). **Long head of biceps (LHB) tendinopathy** is pain at the front of the shoulder from this tendon. It often occurs together with rotator cuff problems [Ref - to verify].

The tendon can also rupture. A **proximal long head rupture** often happens in older adults and causes a visible bulge (the Popeye sign) but frequently has limited loss of function. A **distal biceps rupture** at the elbow is different and usually needs a surgical opinion [Ref - to verify].

items: Pain at the front of the shoulder, sometimes spreading down the front of the arm.

Tenderness over the groove at the front of the shoulder.
After rupture: a sudden pop or tearing, bruising, a bulge in the upper arm, and often a short period of pain followed by less pain.

Any neck pain or arm symptoms?
Any chest pain or breathlessness with front shoulder pain?
Any steroid or fluoroquinolone antibiotic use?

blocks.text: E3. Palpation of the bicipital groove
Palpate along the groove. **Positive:** local tenderness that reproduces the familiar pain. Tenderness alone is common and not specific.

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Sudden pop at the elbow with weak forearm supination and flexion, young or active person
Distal tendon rupture; surgery timing matters
Proximal rupture with severe weakness or in a high-demand worker or athlete
Numbness or weakness in the arm

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
Sudden pop with bulge in the upper arm? **Yes:** suspect rupture. Check the elbow for distal rupture, and refer as needed.
Front shoulder pain with groove tenderness, positive Speed or Yergason, no instability or cuff weakness? **Yes:** working diagnosis is LHB tendinopathy, often with associated cuff problems.
Other findings suggest labral or subscapularis problems? **Yes:** refer for further assessment.
Otherwise: start exercise-based care.

rows: Soft-tissue work for surrounding muscles (pectoralis, deltoid, upper trapezius)
Direct deep friction over the tendon

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** education and load-based exercise. Manual therapy is a minor adjunct only. Do not claim that manual therapy repairs the tendon.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

rows: Isometric elbow flexion with the arm at the side
Sitting, elbow bent to 90 degrees, push the wrist up into the other hand or a surface
5 holds of 30 to 45 seconds [Ref - to verify]
Pain stays high into the next day
Light dumbbell, 3 seconds up, 3 seconds down

blocks.text: **Symptom rule:** pain up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 that settles within a day is acceptable. Avoid heavy pulling or lifting at end range until pain settles.

**After proximal rupture:** most people recover good function with rehabilitation. Start with pain-guided movement, then strengthening of the remaining muscles and a graded return to lifting. Tell the patient that the bulge usually remains [Ref - to verify].
**Distal rupture or surgery:** follow the surgeon's protocol.

rows: Use with caution; tendon rupture risk discussed in some reports [Ref - to verify]

items: **Visit 1:** screen flags, check for rupture, explain the likely cause and plan.
**Early:** reduce painful pulling and lifting, begin isometrics.
**Middle:** slow loaded strengthening, cuff and scapular work.
**Late:** return to work or sport with graded load.
**If no improvement:** review diagnosis and consider imaging and specialist opinion.

blocks.text: Track pain scale, groove tenderness, Speed and Yergason response, elbow flexion and supination strength, function and an outcome measure such as QuickDASH [Ref - to verify].

**Case:** A 58-year-old carpenter has 6 weeks of front shoulder pain with lifting and overhead work. The bicipital groove is tender. Speed's test reproduces his pain. Painful arc is mild, passive range is full, no apprehension, no neurological signs.

**Working diagnosis:** long head of biceps tendinopathy with possible mild cuff involvement. **Plan:** education, isometrics, slow loaded elbow flexion and cuff and scapular strengthening, graded return to overhead work.

items: Why is Speed's test not definitive? It is also positive with other conditions and its accuracy is limited, so it must be combined with palpation and the rest of the examination.

A 62-year-old has a sudden pop and a Popeye bulge but keeps good strength. What is the usual approach? Proximal rupture is often managed without surgery in older, less demanding patients; reassure and rehabilitate [Ref - to verify].
Why check the elbow after a pop in the arm? A distal rupture changes urgency because earlier surgical review may be needed.
Why avoid steroid injection near the tendon? Some reports link it with tendon weakening and rupture [Ref - to verify].
Why is heart pain on the list? Front shoulder or arm pain can come from the heart and must be excluded in the right history.
**Initial approach:** education and progressive tendon loading.
**Justifying findings:** front shoulder pain, groove tenderness, positive Speed or Yergason, no flags.
**Priority:** tendon capacity and function.
**Manual therapy:** minor adjunct.
**Exercise:** isometrics, slow loaded elbow flexion, cuff and scapular strengthening.
**Modalities:** limited role.
**Tell the patient:** common and treatable; a rupture bulge is usually cosmetic with good function.
**Avoid:** heavy lifting at end range early, direct friction, delaying referral for distal rupture.
**Measure:** pain, strength, function, QuickDASH.
**If no improvement:** specialist review.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** function restored and strengthening habit established.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** adult, no instability, no major cuff tear.

items: **Can be tested:** whether exercise therapy helps LHB tendinopathy; outcomes of surgery versus conservative care for proximal and distal rupture.
**Hypotheses:** that slow heavy loading improves tendon capacity.
**Future questions:** which patients need surgery for the long head of biceps.
